title: Why it's safe
prompt: Sorted array, `nums[l] + nums[r] < target`. Why is `l++` correct (not skipping any answer)?
options: r is the largest remaining value, so if even nums[l]+nums[r] is too small, l pairs with nothing — discard l
Because we always move the left pointer on ties
It isn't — you must check all pairs
explanation: Each move permanently eliminates one endpoint with a proof it can't be in the answer. That's what makes two pointers O(n) instead of O(n²) — and why it needs sorted input.

title: Drill: converging pointers
prompt: From memory: return whether `nums` reads the same forwards and backwards (an array palindrome). The converging while-loop template, no copies allowed.

solution.explanation: Position i must equal position n-1-i; converging pointers check every mirrored pair once and stop at the centre (l < r, so odd lengths skip the middle). O(n) time, O(1) space.

hints: A palindrome mirrors around its centre. Which pairs of positions must match?
Start one index at each end and walk them toward each other.
`while (l < r) { if (nums[l] != nums[r]) return false; l++; r--; }`

title: Drill: dedup a sorted array (same-direction)
prompt: From memory (slow/fast, same direction): remove duplicates from the SORTED array `nums` in place so each value appears once, and return the new length. The first `length` elements of nums must hold the unique values.

solution.explanation: In a sorted array a value is new exactly when it differs from the last kept value, so `nums[0..slow]` is always the deduplicated prefix. Each element is visited once by `fast`. O(n) time, O(1) space.

hints: Because the array is sorted, duplicates sit next to each other. How do you know a value is new?
Keep a `slow` index at the last unique value; scan with `fast` and copy only values that differ from `nums[slow]`.
On a new value: `slow++; nums[slow] = nums[fast];` — return `slow + 1`.

title: Template recall: converging pointers
prompt: From memory: the Two Sum II template on a sorted array.
explanation: Start at both ends and loop while the pointers are distinct. A sum that is too small can only grow by moving `l` right; a sum that is too large can only shrink by moving `r` left. Each move discards one index for good: O(n).

title: Which wall moves?
prompt: Container With Most Water: `height[l] = 2`, `height[r] = 7`, width `r - l = 5` (area 10). Why is `l++` the right move?
options: Every other container using `l` is narrower and still capped at height 2, so none beats 10 — `l` can be discarded
Moving the taller wall could find a taller one, which always increases the area
We always move the left pointer first
Because 2 < 7 means the answer is on the right half
explanation: The shorter wall caps the height of any container that uses it, and every remaining partner is closer (narrower). So the container just measured is the best `l` will ever be part of. Moving the taller wall instead keeps the cap at 2 while shrinking width — it can never help.
